questions.q: Which volcano in Washington State erupted in 1980, blowing off its top?
questions.fact: The eruption lowered the mountain by about 400 meters.

questions.q: Which Indonesian volcano's 1883 eruption was heard thousands of kilometers away?
questions.fact: It is often called one of the loudest sounds in recorded history.

questions.q: Which Indonesian volcano erupted in 1815 and caused the Year Without a Summer?
questions.fact: Ash in the sky cooled the planet, and snow fell in New England in June 1816.

questions.q: Which is the tallest mountain on Earth when measured from its base on the ocean floor?
questions.fact: Mauna Kea in Hawaii is over 10,000 meters from base to top, but most of it is underwater.

questions.q: Which point on Earth is farthest from the planet's center?
questions.fact: Earth bulges at the equator, so Chimborazo in Ecuador sticks out the farthest.

questions.q: Which is the deepest part of the ocean?
choices: The bottom of the Red Sea
Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench
questions.fact: It is about 11 kilometers deep, deeper than Mount Everest is tall.

questions.q: Who were the first people to reach the bottom of the Mariana Trench, in 1960?
questions.fact: They dove in a vessel called the Trieste, and filmmaker James Cameron made a solo dive there in 2012.

questions.q: What is the world's longest mountain range, mostly underwater?
questions.fact: The Mid-Ocean Ridge winds about 65,000 kilometers around the globe.

questions.q: What percentage of Earth's surface is covered by water?
questions.fact: That is why Earth is often called the Blue Planet.

questions.q: About what percent of Earth's water is salt water in the oceans?
questions.fact: Only about 3 percent of Earth's water is fresh, and most of that is frozen in ice.

questions.q: Where is most of Earth's fresh water stored?
questions.fact: The Antarctic ice sheet alone holds most of the world's fresh water.

questions.q: Why is the ocean salty?
choices: Rivers carry dissolved minerals from rocks into the sea
questions.fact: When ocean water evaporates, the salt stays behind, so it builds up over time.

questions.q: How many oceans does Earth have, as most geographers count them today?
questions.fact: They are the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic oceans.

questions.q: Which ocean is the second largest?
questions.fact: The Atlantic Ocean is getting wider by a few centimeters each year.

questions.q: Which warm ocean current flows from the Gulf of Mexico across the Atlantic toward Europe?
questions.fact: The Gulf Stream helps keep parts of Western Europe milder than other places as far north.

questions.q: What is the name for the rising and falling of the sea level twice a day?
questions.fact: Most coasts have two high tides and two low tides about every 24 hours and 50 minutes.

questions.q: What causes most ocean waves?
questions.fact: The longer and harder the wind blows, the bigger the waves get.

questions.q: What is the largest coral reef system in the world?
questions.fact: It stretches over 2,000 kilometers and can be seen from space.

questions.q: What happens to coral when the water gets too warm?
choices: It can turn white, called coral bleaching
questions.fact: Bleached coral has lost the tiny algae that give it food and color.

questions.q: What is the zone of the ocean too deep for any sunlight to reach called?
questions.fact: In the midnight zone, the only light comes from glowing animals.

questions.q: What are hot springs on the deep sea floor where strange creatures live called?
questions.fact: Giant tube worms near vents live without sunlight, getting food from bacteria.

questions.q: What is the longest river in the world?
questions.fact: Some scientists argue the Amazon is longer, depending on how its source is measured.

questions.q: What is the place where a river begins called?
questions.fact: The place where a river ends, usually at a sea or lake, is called its mouth.

questions.q: What is the area of land that drains into one river called?
questions.fact: Everything that falls on a watershed eventually drains toward the same river.

questions.q: What is an underground layer of rock that holds water called?
questions.fact: Wells pump water up from aquifers.

questions.q: What do we call a swampy, wet land area like a marsh or bog?
questions.fact: Wetlands soak up floodwater like a giant sponge.

questions.q: What is the large wetland in southern Florida famous for alligators called?
questions.fact: The Everglades is sometimes called a river of grass.

questions.q: What are the large areas with similar climate, plants and animals, like deserts and rainforests, called?
questions.fact: Major biomes include tundra, desert, grassland, forest and rainforest.

questions.q: What is the huge forest of evergreen trees across Canada, Scandinavia and Russia called?
questions.fact: The taiga, or boreal forest, is the largest land biome on Earth.

questions.q: What is the grassland with scattered trees in Africa called?
questions.fact: Lions, zebras and elephants live on the African savanna.

questions.q: What are the grasslands of North America called?
questions.fact: Huge herds of bison once roamed the prairies.

questions.q: What do we call ground that stays frozen all year in very cold places?
questions.fact: As permafrost thaws, it can release greenhouse gases.

questions.q: What is the largest tropical rainforest on Earth?
questions.fact: The Amazon is home to about one in ten known species on Earth.

questions.q: What is the top layer of a rainforest, where most branches and leaves spread out, called?
questions.fact: The canopy can block so much light that the forest floor is dark even at noon.

questions.q: What is a desert?
choices: A place that gets very little rain
A place covered in sand only
questions.fact: Antarctica counts as a desert because it gets so little snow and rain.

questions.q: What is the largest desert in the world, counting cold deserts?
questions.fact: The Sahara is the largest hot desert.

questions.q: Which desert in South America is one of the driest places on Earth?
questions.fact: Some weather stations in the Atacama have almost never recorded rain.

questions.q: In which desert is Death Valley, one of the hottest places on Earth?
questions.fact: Death Valley in California recorded about 56.7 degrees Celsius in 1913.

questions.q: What is the name of a big desert in Mongolia and China famous for dinosaur fossils?
questions.fact: The first dinosaur egg nests were found in the Gobi in the 1920s.

questions.q: What is a scientist who studies weather called?
questions.fact: Meteorologists study the atmosphere, not meteors.

questions.q: What is the difference between weather and climate?
choices: Weather is day to day, climate is the long-term pattern
questions.fact: You could say climate is what you expect and weather is what you get.

questions.q: What is the layer of gases around Earth called?
questions.fact: Most of the atmosphere's air is in the lowest 16 kilometers or so.

questions.q: Which layer of the atmosphere do most planes fly in or just above?
questions.fact: Planes fly high to stay above most of the bumpy weather.

questions.q: In which layer of the atmosphere do most meteors burn up?
questions.fact: The mesosphere is the coldest layer of the atmosphere.

questions.q: What instrument measures wind speed?
questions.fact: Many anemometers have spinning cups that turn faster in stronger wind.

questions.q: What instrument shows which way the wind is blowing?
questions.fact: A wind vane points toward the direction the wind is coming from.

questions.q: What instrument measures how much rain has fallen?
questions.fact: A rain gauge is basically a cup with measuring marks.

questions.q: What scale describes wind strength by what it does, from calm to hurricane?
questions.fact: It was created in 1805 by Francis Beaufort, a British navy officer.

questions.q: Which scale rates hurricanes from Category 1 to Category 5?
questions.fact: A Category 5 hurricane has winds of at least 252 kilometers per hour.

questions.q: Which scale is used to rate tornadoes by their damage?
questions.fact: It goes from EF0, the weakest, to EF5, the most violent.

questions.q: What are high, thin, wispy clouds made of ice crystals called?
questions.fact: Cirrus means curl of hair in Latin.

questions.q: What are puffy white clouds that look like cotton balls called?
questions.fact: Cumulus means heap or pile in Latin.

questions.q: What are flat, gray clouds that cover the sky like a blanket called?
questions.fact: Stratus clouds often bring drizzle or gloomy days.

questions.q: What is fog?
questions.fact: Fog forms when air near the ground cools and its water vapor condenses.

questions.q: What are clouds made of?
choices: Tiny water droplets or ice crystals
questions.fact: A puffy cumulus cloud can weigh as much as about 100 elephants.

questions.q: What is the water that collects on grass on cool mornings called?
questions.fact: Dew forms when moist air touches surfaces that cooled down overnight.

questions.q: What is the temperature at which air becomes full of moisture and dew forms called?
questions.fact: When the dew point is high, the air feels sticky and humid.

questions.q: What do we call balls of ice that fall from thunderstorms?
questions.fact: The largest hailstone recorded in the United States fell in South Dakota in 2010 and was about 20 centimeters wide.

questions.q: What is rain that freezes into ice pellets before reaching the ground called?
questions.fact: Sleet bounces when it hits the ground.

questions.q: What shape do snowflakes almost always have?
questions.fact: The six-sided shape comes from how water molecules link together when they freeze.

questions.q: What is a storm with strong winds and lots of blowing snow called?
questions.fact: A storm counts as a blizzard when blowing snow makes it very hard to see for hours.

questions.q: What is a long period with much less rain than usual called?
questions.fact: Droughts can dry up crops, rivers and lakes.

questions.q: What is a seasonal wind that brings heavy rains to South Asia called?
questions.fact: Farmers in India depend on monsoon rains for their crops.

questions.q: What is a violently spinning column of air that reaches from a storm cloud to the ground?
questions.fact: The fastest tornado winds can be more than 400 kilometers per hour.

questions.q: Which country has the most tornadoes in the world?
questions.fact: The United States has more than 1,000 tornadoes in a typical year.

questions.q: What is the region in the central United States known for many tornadoes?
questions.fact: Tornado Alley stretches across states like Texas, Oklahoma and Kansas.

questions.q: What is a giant spinning storm over the Atlantic Ocean with winds over 119 kilometers per hour called?
questions.fact: Hurricanes are called typhoons in the western Pacific and cyclones in the Indian Ocean.

questions.q: What is the calm area at the center of a hurricane called?
questions.fact: Inside the eye, the sky can be clear and the wind gentle, but the strongest winds surround it.

questions.q: What do hurricanes need to form?
questions.fact: Hurricanes weaken quickly after they move over land or cold water.

questions.q: Which way do hurricanes spin in the Northern Hemisphere?
questions.fact: In the Southern Hemisphere, they spin clockwise because of Earth's rotation.

questions.q: What is the effect that makes storms spin because of Earth's rotation called?
questions.fact: The Coriolis effect is too weak to decide which way water drains in a sink.

questions.q: Which weather event kills more people in the United States than tornadoes in most years?
questions.fact: Heat waves are often called the silent killer because they do not look scary.

questions.q: How hot can a lightning bolt be?
questions.fact: That is about five times hotter than the surface of the Sun.

questions.q: About how many times does lightning strike Earth every second?
questions.fact: That adds up to about 4 million lightning strikes a day.

questions.q: Can lightning strike the same place twice?
choices: Yes, and tall buildings get hit often
questions.fact: The Empire State Building is struck by lightning about 20 times a year.

questions.q: What is the safest place to be during a thunderstorm?
choices: Inside a building or a hard-topped car
questions.fact: A good rule is when thunder roars, go indoors.

questions.q: What causes wind?
choices: Air moving from high pressure to low pressure
questions.fact: Uneven heating of Earth by the Sun creates these differences in pressure.

questions.q: What is a sea breeze?
choices: Cool wind blowing from the sea to the land on sunny days
Wind blowing from land to sea at noon
questions.fact: Land heats up faster than water, so the air over land rises and cool sea air rushes in.

questions.q: What are fast rivers of air high in the atmosphere that planes use to fly faster called?
questions.fact: Flights from the United States to Europe are often faster because of the jet stream.

questions.q: What were the steady winds that sailing ships used to cross oceans called?
questions.fact: Trade winds blow toward the equator from the east.

questions.q: What is the calm area near the equator where sailing ships often got stuck called?
questions.fact: Being in the doldrums now also means feeling bored or stuck.

questions.q: What is the hottest temperature ever recorded on Earth?
questions.fact: It was recorded in Death Valley, California, in 1913, though some scientists question the measurement.

questions.q: Where was the coldest air temperature on Earth's surface measured?
questions.fact: In 1983 it reached minus 89.2 degrees Celsius.

questions.q: What is the line of latitude at 0 degrees called?
questions.fact: Places near the equator have warm weather all year.

questions.q: What is the line of longitude at 0 degrees, running through Greenwich, England, called?
questions.fact: Longitude lines run from the North Pole to the South Pole.

questions.q: What do lines of latitude measure?
choices: How far north or south of the equator a place is
How far east or west a place is
questions.fact: The North Pole is at 90 degrees north latitude.

questions.q: What happens at the North Pole in summer?
choices: It is the hottest place on Earth
The Sun stays up all day and night
questions.fact: This is why the Arctic is called the land of the midnight sun.

questions.q: What do we call the imaginary lines on a globe that help find exact locations?
questions.fact: Every place on Earth has its own latitude and longitude.

questions.q: Which line is roughly where one calendar day changes to the next?
questions.fact: It zigzags through the Pacific Ocean to avoid splitting countries.

questions.q: Is the South Pole on land or on ice floating on the ocean?
choices: On a mountain of rock with no ice
questions.fact: The ice at the South Pole is about 2,700 meters thick.

questions.q: Is the North Pole on land?
choices: No, it is on floating sea ice
questions.fact: Submarines have traveled under the ice at the North Pole.

questions.q: About how tall is Mount Everest?
questions.fact: Mount Everest is on the border between Nepal and China.

questions.q: What is the tallest mountain in Africa?
questions.fact: Kilimanjaro is a dormant volcano in Tanzania with snow near its top.

questions.q: What are the Seven Summits?
choices: The highest mountain on each continent
questions.fact: Climbing all seven is a big challenge for mountaineers.

questions.q: Which is the longest mountain range above water?
questions.fact: The Andes run about 7,000 kilometers along South America.

questions.q: What is the line above which snow stays on a mountain all year called?
questions.fact: Near the equator, the snow line is much higher than near the poles.

questions.q: What is the line on a mountain above which trees cannot grow called?
questions.fact: Above the tree line it is too cold and windy for trees.

questions.q: What are huge sheets of ice covering land, like in Antarctica and Greenland, called?
questions.fact: If all of Antarctica's ice melted, sea levels would rise by about 58 meters.

questions.q: What is a big chunk of ice that breaks off a glacier and floats in the sea called?
questions.fact: About 90 percent of an iceberg is hidden under the water.

questions.q: What is it called when a chunk of ice breaks off a glacier into the water?
questions.fact: Calving can make big splashes and even small tsunamis.

questions.q: What do we call a long period when ice sheets covered much more of Earth?
questions.fact: The last big ice age peaked about 20,000 years ago.

questions.q: What are the piles of rocks and dirt left behind by glaciers called?
questions.fact: Long Island in New York is partly made of glacier moraines.

questions.q: Which huge island is mostly covered by an ice sheet, even though its name sounds green?
questions.fact: Greenland is the world's largest island that is not a continent.

questions.q: How old is the Earth?
questions.fact: The oldest minerals found on Earth are tiny zircon crystals about 4.4 billion years old.

questions.q: What were the first living things on Earth like?
questions.fact: Simple microbes appeared at least 3.5 billion years ago.

questions.q: What were the tiny ocean microbes that first filled Earth's air with oxygen?
questions.fact: Their oxygen buildup is called the Great Oxidation Event, about 2.4 billion years ago.

questions.q: Which era is known as the Age of Dinosaurs?
questions.fact: The Mesozoic is split into the Triassic, Jurassic and Cretaceous periods.

questions.q: Which era are we living in now?
questions.fact: The Cenozoic Era began about 66 million years ago, after the dinosaurs died out.

questions.q: What is amber?
questions.fact: Insects trapped in amber millions of years ago can still be seen inside it.

questions.q: What is a fossil of a footprint, burrow or nest called?
questions.fact: Trace fossils tell scientists how ancient animals moved and lived.

questions.q: What does the law of superposition say about rock layers?
choices: All layers are the same age
questions.fact: It works like a pile of laundry, the bottom was put there first.

questions.q: What is soil made of?
choices: Bits of rock, rotted plants and animals, air and water
questions.fact: It can take hundreds of years to form just a few centimeters of soil.

questions.q: What is the dark, rich part of soil made from rotted plants and animals called?
questions.fact: Humus helps soil hold water and feeds plants.

questions.q: What type of soil has the tiniest particles and gets sticky when wet?
questions.fact: Clay can be shaped and baked into bricks and pottery.

questions.q: What is the best soil for growing most plants, a mix of sand, silt and clay?
questions.fact: Loam drains well but still holds enough water for roots.

questions.q: What is the solid rock under the soil called?
questions.fact: Bedrock can be just under the surface or many meters down.

questions.q: What do farmers plant to hold soil in place and stop erosion?
questions.fact: During the Dust Bowl in the 1930s, plowed prairie soil blew away in giant dust storms.

questions.q: What was the Dust Bowl?
choices: Huge dust storms on the US Great Plains in the 1930s
questions.fact: Poor farming and drought let the wind blow away tons of dry soil.

questions.q: What is the gradual warming of Earth's average temperature called?
questions.fact: As of 2025, the last ten years have been the warmest on record.

questions.q: What is the main human cause of climate change?
questions.fact: Burning coal, oil and gas adds carbon dioxide that traps heat.

questions.q: Why are sea levels rising?
choices: Melting ice and warming water expanding
questions.fact: Water takes up more space as it warms.

questions.q: What thin layer of gas in the stratosphere was being damaged by chemicals called CFCs?
questions.fact: After CFCs were banned by the 1987 Montreal Protocol, the ozone layer began slowly healing.

questions.q: Over which place did a large hole in the ozone layer form each spring?
questions.fact: The ozone hole is expected to mostly recover by around 2066 over Antarctica.

questions.q: What is acid rain?
choices: Rain made acidic by pollution in the air
questions.fact: Acid rain can damage forests, lakes and stone statues.

questions.q: What is the brownish haze of air pollution over cities called?
questions.fact: The word smog was made by joining smoke and fog.

questions.q: What is it called when forests are cut down and not replaced?
questions.fact: Trees take in carbon dioxide, so cutting them down adds to climate change.

questions.q: What is planting trees where a forest was lost called?
questions.fact: A single large tree can take in more than 20 kilograms of carbon dioxide a year.

questions.q: What is the floating mass of plastic trash in the Pacific Ocean called?
questions.fact: Most of it is tiny bits of plastic, not a solid island you could walk on.

questions.q: What are the three Rs of helping the environment?
questions.fact: Reducing comes first because the best trash is the trash you never make.

questions.q: What is composting?
choices: Turning food scraps and leaves into rich soil
questions.fact: Worms and microbes do most of the work in a compost pile.

questions.q: What do we call energy from sources that will not run out, like the Sun and wind?
questions.fact: As of 2025, solar power is the fastest-growing source of electricity in the world.

questions.q: Which natural resource is formed from tiny sea creatures buried for millions of years?
questions.fact: Oil and natural gas mostly come from ancient ocean plankton.

questions.q: Where is most of Earth's liquid fresh water found?
questions.fact: Groundwater fills the spaces between rocks and soil underground.

questions.q: What do we call the process of making salt water drinkable?
questions.fact: Countries in the Middle East get much of their drinking water from desalination plants.

questions.q: What do we call water that has drained off land into rivers and streams?
questions.fact: Runoff can carry dirt and chemicals from farms and streets into rivers.

questions.q: In the water cycle, what is it called when water vapor turns into clouds?
questions.fact: The water you drink may once have been drunk by a dinosaur, because water keeps cycling.

questions.q: What powers the water cycle?
questions.fact: The Sun evaporates huge amounts of water from the oceans every day.

questions.q: What is a flood that happens very quickly, often after heavy rain, called?
questions.fact: Just 15 centimeters of fast-moving water can knock an adult off their feet.

questions.q: What is a sudden slide of rocks and soil down a hill called?
questions.fact: Heavy rain, earthquakes and cutting down hillside trees can cause landslides.

questions.q: What is a large mass of snow sliding fast down a mountain called?
questions.fact: Avalanches can travel more than 300 kilometers per hour.

questions.q: What is a wildfire?
questions.fact: Some trees, like certain pines, need fire's heat to open their cones and spread seeds.

questions.q: Why is Earth's magnetic field important to living things?
choices: It helps shield Earth from harmful solar particles
questions.fact: Without it, the solar wind could strip away much of the atmosphere over time.

questions.q: Do Earth's magnetic poles ever swap places?
choices: Yes, many times in the past
questions.fact: Rocks on the sea floor record these flips like a striped barcode.

questions.q: What is the name for the outer rigid shell of Earth made of the crust and upper mantle?
questions.fact: The lithosphere is broken into the tectonic plates.

questions.q: What is the name for all of Earth's water, including oceans, lakes and ice?
questions.fact: Hydro comes from the Greek word for water.

questions.q: What is the name for all the living things on Earth together?
questions.fact: The biosphere reaches from deep underground to high in the sky.

questions.q: What gives Earth's sky its colors during sunrise and sunset?
questions.fact: Dust and pollution can make sunsets even more colorful.

questions.q: How long does Earth take to spin once on its axis?
questions.fact: Earth actually spins once every 23 hours and 56 minutes compared with the stars.

questions.q: About how fast does a point on the equator move as Earth spins?
questions.fact: We do not feel it because everything around us moves along with us.

questions.q: What shape is Earth?
choices: A sphere that bulges a little at the equator
questions.fact: Earth's spin makes it about 43 kilometers wider around the equator than from pole to pole.

questions.q: About how far is it around Earth at the equator?
questions.fact: An ancient Greek scientist named Eratosthenes estimated it closely more than 2,000 years ago.

questions.q: Which ancient Greek scientist measured Earth's size using shadows and wells?
questions.fact: He compared shadows in two Egyptian cities to calculate Earth's circumference.

questions.q: Why do we have leap years?
choices: To give February more days for fun
Earth takes about 365 and a quarter days to orbit the Sun
questions.fact: Adding a day every four years keeps the calendar matched with the seasons.

questions.q: When it is summer in the United States, what season is it in Australia?
questions.fact: The Northern and Southern Hemispheres have opposite seasons.

questions.q: What do we call the season between summer and winter?
questions.fact: Autumn is also called fall in the United States because leaves fall from trees.

questions.q: Why do leaves change color in autumn?
choices: Green chlorophyll breaks down and other colors show
questions.fact: Shorter days and cooler nights tell trees to stop making chlorophyll.

questions.q: Why do some places near the equator have only wet and dry seasons?
choices: They get strong sunlight all year
questions.fact: Near the equator, temperatures stay warm, so rain is what changes most.

questions.q: What is the gemstone form of the mineral corundum that is red?
questions.fact: Blue corundum is called sapphire.

questions.q: What is a blue gemstone made of the mineral corundum?
questions.fact: Sapphires can also be pink, yellow and many other colors.

questions.q: What is a green gemstone that is a type of the mineral beryl?
questions.fact: Most emeralds have tiny flaws inside, which jewelers call the garden.

questions.q: What is a purple gemstone made of quartz?
questions.fact: The name comes from a Greek word, because people once believed it stopped drunkenness.

questions.q: Which gemstone forms inside oysters instead of in the ground?
questions.fact: Pearls are one of the few gems made by living animals.

questions.q: How do diamonds usually reach Earth's surface?
choices: Carried up by deep volcanic eruptions
questions.fact: Most diamonds formed more than 150 kilometers underground over a billion years ago.

questions.q: What is the largest gem-quality diamond ever found?
questions.fact: It was found in South Africa in 1905 and cut into stones for the British Crown Jewels.

questions.q: Which famous blue diamond is in the Smithsonian museum and rumored to be cursed?
questions.fact: The Hope Diamond glows red-orange for a while after being exposed to ultraviolet light.

questions.q: What is an ore?
choices: Rock containing enough metal to be worth mining
questions.fact: Iron ore is melted in furnaces to make iron and steel.

questions.q: Which metal ore is the main source of aluminum?
questions.fact: Australia is one of the world's biggest producers of bauxite.

questions.q: Which mineral, used for rock salt, is mined from the ground?
questions.fact: Halite is the mineral name for table salt.

questions.q: Which soft mineral is used to make plaster and drywall?
questions.fact: A cave in Mexico called the Cave of the Crystals has gypsum crystals longer than a bus.

questions.q: Which flaky mineral splits into thin, see-through sheets?
questions.fact: Mica was once used for windows in stoves and lanterns.

questions.q: What lies under Yellowstone National Park?
questions.fact: Yellowstone sits on top of a huge hot spot of magma deep underground.

questions.q: What are hot spots in Earth's mantle known for creating?
choices: Chains of volcanic islands like Hawaii
questions.fact: As the plate moves over the hot spot, new islands form in a line.

questions.q: Which Hawaiian volcano has been one of the most active in the world?
questions.fact: In Hawaiian tradition, Kilauea is home to Pele, the goddess of fire and volcanoes.

questions.q: What is the name for volcanic rock fragments that fly through the air during an eruption?
questions.fact: Tephra includes everything from fine ash to huge volcanic bombs.

questions.q: What is a fast, deadly cloud of hot gas and rock that rushes down a volcano called?
questions.fact: Pyroclastic flows can move faster than 100 kilometers per hour.

questions.q: What are volcanic mudflows called?
questions.fact: Lahars form when volcanic ash mixes with water from rain or melting snow.

questions.q: Which island country formed on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge has many volcanoes and geysers?
questions.fact: In Iceland, you can stand where the North American and Eurasian plates are pulling apart.

questions.q: Which new island formed from an undersea volcano near Iceland in 1963?
questions.fact: Scientists have studied Surtsey to see how plants and animals arrive on brand-new land.

questions.q: Which Japanese mountain is a famous volcano?
questions.fact: Mount Fuji last erupted in 1707.

questions.q: Which Philippine volcano's 1991 eruption cooled the whole planet for about a year?
questions.fact: It threw so much gas into the stratosphere that global temperatures dropped about half a degree Celsius.

questions.q: Which large lake in Central Asia has mostly dried up because its rivers were used to water crops?
questions.fact: The Aral Sea was once one of the four largest lakes in the world.

questions.q: Which sea has no coastline at all?
questions.fact: The Sargasso Sea in the Atlantic is defined by ocean currents and floating seaweed.

questions.q: What is a strait?
choices: A narrow channel of water connecting two larger bodies of water
questions.fact: The Strait of Gibraltar separates Europe from Africa.

questions.q: What is a lagoon?
choices: Shallow water separated from the sea by a reef or sandbar
questions.fact: Venice, Italy, was built on islands in a lagoon.

questions.q: What are the steep rocky walls along a coast, worn by waves, called?
questions.fact: Waves can carve sea cliffs into arches and tall stacks of rock.

questions.q: What is a natural rock arch along a coast eventually likely to become?
questions.fact: When the top of the arch collapses, the pillar left standing is called a stack.

questions.q: What are most beaches made of?
questions.fact: Some Hawaiian beaches have black sand made from volcanic rock.

questions.q: What is the pink sand on some beaches in Bermuda partly made of?
choices: Tiny red shells of sea creatures
questions.fact: The tiny creatures are called foraminifera.

questions.q: What do you call a large, slow-moving swirl of ocean currents?
questions.fact: Garbage patches form in the middle of gyres.

questions.q: What is a powerful swirling body of water, like in some narrow sea passages, called?
questions.fact: The Saltstraumen in Norway is one of the strongest tidal currents in the world.

questions.q: What is a rip current?
choices: A strong current pulling water away from the beach
questions.fact: If caught in one, swim parallel to the shore until you are out of it.

questions.q: How deep can sunlight reach in the ocean?
questions.fact: Below 1,000 meters, it is completely dark.

questions.q: How much of the ocean have people mapped in high detail, as of 2025?
questions.fact: As of 2025, about a quarter of the sea floor has been mapped in high detail.

questions.q: What color does deep, clear ocean water look, and why?
choices: Blue, because water absorbs red light
questions.fact: Water absorbs red, orange and yellow light, leaving mostly blue.

questions.q: What makes some lakes look bright turquoise?
questions.fact: This fine dust is called rock flour.

questions.q: What is the place where a river's fresh water mixes with the sea's salt water called?
questions.fact: Estuaries are rich nurseries for young fish.

questions.q: What is a curving bend in a river called?
questions.fact: When a meander gets cut off, it can become an oxbow lake.

questions.q: What is the flat land beside a river that floods sometimes called?
questions.fact: Floodplains have very rich soil because floods leave behind mud.

questions.q: What is a lake made by people when they build a dam called?
questions.fact: Many cities get their drinking water from reservoirs.

questions.q: Which river flows through Egypt and helped ancient Egyptians farm?
questions.fact: Its yearly floods left fertile mud along the riverbanks.

questions.q: Which river is the longest in the United States?
questions.fact: The Missouri is slightly longer than the Mississippi, which it flows into.

questions.q: What is the largest canyon in the world by some measures, in Tibet?
questions.fact: It is deeper than the Grand Canyon in Arizona.

questions.q: What is the giant red sandstone rock in the middle of Australia, sacred to Aboriginal people, called?
questions.fact: Uluru seems to change color, glowing bright red at sunrise and sunset.

questions.q: What is the huge crack in East Africa where the continent is slowly splitting apart called?
questions.fact: In millions of years, eastern Africa may break off to form a new landmass.

questions.q: Which large mountain range separates Europe and Asia?
questions.fact: The Ural Mountains are very old and have been worn down by erosion.

questions.q: Which mountain range in Europe includes Mont Blanc?
questions.fact: Mont Blanc is the tallest mountain in the Alps.

questions.q: How much of the Sahara is covered by sand dunes?
questions.fact: Most of the Sahara is rocky plains and gravel.

questions.q: Was the Sahara Desert always a desert?
choices: No, it was green with lakes thousands of years ago
It used to be an ocean last century
It used to be covered in ice last century
questions.fact: Ancient rock art in the Sahara shows giraffes and hippos.

questions.q: What is the large region of Earth near the equator that is warm all year called?
questions.fact: The tropics lie between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn.

questions.q: What do we call the climate zones between the tropics and the polar regions, with four seasons?
questions.fact: Most of the United States and Europe are in the temperate zone.

questions.q: What is the climate of most rainforests?
choices: Dry for half the year with snow
questions.fact: Some rainforests get more than 2.5 meters of rain a year.

questions.q: What kind of climate does the Mediterranean region have?
choices: Hot dry summers and mild wet winters
questions.fact: California, parts of Chile and South Africa have Mediterranean climates too.

questions.q: Why are mountaintops colder than valleys?
choices: They are closer to space ice
Air gets thinner and cooler higher up
questions.fact: Temperatures often drop about 6.5 degrees Celsius for every kilometer you climb.

questions.q: Why are places near the ocean often milder than places far inland?
choices: The ocean makes its own heat
questions.fact: This is why coastal cities usually have cooler summers and warmer winters.

questions.q: What is a heat wave?
choices: Several days of unusually hot weather
A wave in a hot tub
questions.fact: Drinking water and staying in shade help people stay safe in a heat wave.

questions.q: What is El Niño?
choices: A warming of the Pacific Ocean that changes weather around the world
questions.fact: El Niño means the boy in Spanish, because fishermen noticed it around Christmas.

questions.q: What is the cooling of the Pacific Ocean, opposite to El Niño, called?
questions.fact: La Niña means the girl in Spanish.

questions.q: What does a weather forecast use to predict the weather?
choices: Data from satellites, radar and weather stations
questions.fact: Supercomputers run weather models millions of times faster than people could.

questions.q: What does weather radar mainly detect?
choices: Rain, snow and hail in clouds
questions.fact: Radar sends out radio waves that bounce off raindrops and come back.

questions.q: What is a cold front?
choices: The edge of a cold air mass pushing into warmer air
questions.fact: Cold fronts often bring thunderstorms and then cooler, clearer weather.

questions.q: What weather does high air pressure usually bring?
questions.fact: Low pressure often brings clouds, wind and rain.

questions.q: What is the windiest continent on Earth?
questions.fact: Winds pouring down off the Antarctic ice can be stronger than hurricane winds.

questions.q: How thick is the ice in Antarctica at its thickest?
questions.fact: The ice sheet is so heavy it pushes the land beneath it down.

questions.q: What is a huge floating shelf of ice attached to the coast of Antarctica called?
questions.fact: The Ross Ice Shelf is about the size of France.

questions.q: What is the name of the largest lake buried under the Antarctic ice?
questions.fact: Lake Vostok is under about 4 kilometers of ice and has been sealed off for millions of years.

questions.q: Which is the coldest place inhabited all year by people, a village in Siberia?
questions.fact: Winter temperatures in Oymyakon can fall below minus 60 degrees Celsius.

questions.q: What does a compass point to on Earth?
questions.fact: Magnetic north is not exactly the same spot as the geographic North Pole, and it slowly moves.

questions.q: Is magnetic north moving?
choices: Yes, it has been drifting toward Siberia
It moves to the equator each summer
questions.fact: Scientists update maps of magnetic north every few years because of this drift.

questions.q: What are topographic maps used to show?
choices: The shape and height of the land
questions.fact: Contour lines that are close together show steep slopes.

questions.q: What does a map scale tell you?
choices: How distances on the map compare to real distances
questions.fact: For example, 1 centimeter on the map might equal 1 kilometer in real life.

questions.q: What is the science of making maps called?
questions.fact: Mapmakers are called cartographers.

questions.q: What is a scientist who studies the ocean called?
questions.fact: Oceanographers study waves, currents, sea life and the sea floor.

questions.q: What is a scientist who studies volcanoes called?
questions.fact: Volcanologists wear heat-resistant suits to get close to lava.

questions.q: What is a scientist who studies earthquakes called?
questions.fact: Seismologists use networks of instruments to find where earthquakes start.

questions.q: What is a scientist who studies glaciers called?
questions.fact: Glaciologists drill ice cores to learn about Earth's past climate.

questions.q: What can ice cores drilled from glaciers tell scientists?
choices: What Earth's air and climate were like long ago
questions.fact: Bubbles trapped in Antarctic ice hold samples of air from about 800,000 years ago.

questions.q: How can tree rings tell us about past weather?
choices: Wide rings mean good growing years, thin rings mean hard years
They show the temperature in numbers
questions.fact: The study of tree rings is called dendrochronology.

questions.q: What are the four main parts of the water cycle?
questions.fact: The same water has been cycling around Earth for billions of years.

questions.q: What is water that soaks into the ground called?
questions.fact: Sandy ground lets water soak in quickly, while clay slows it down.

questions.q: What is a natural place where groundwater flows out onto the surface?
questions.fact: Some springs are hot because the water is heated deep underground.

questions.q: What makes a cloud turn dark gray before rain?
choices: It is so thick with water drops that sunlight cannot get through
questions.fact: Thin clouds look white because light passes through and scatters.

questions.q: Why does it often rain more on one side of a mountain range?
choices: Air rises over the mountains, cools and drops its rain
The other side has no clouds ever
questions.fact: The dry side behind the mountains is called a rain shadow.

questions.q: What is a rain shadow?
choices: A dry area on the far side of mountains
A shadow made by rain clouds
questions.fact: The Atacama Desert and Death Valley are both in rain shadows.

questions.q: Which kind of cloud looks like a flying saucer and forms near mountains?
questions.fact: People have mistaken lenticular clouds for UFOs.

questions.q: What is the rumbling sound that follows lightning called?
questions.fact: Thunder can be heard up to about 15 kilometers from the lightning.

questions.q: What is a waterspout?
questions.fact: Waterspouts often form over warm tropical seas.

questions.q: What is a dust devil?
choices: A small spinning whirlwind of dust on a hot day
A type of tornado that lasts for weeks
questions.fact: Dust devils form when the ground gets very hot and air rises in a spinning column.

questions.q: What is a huge wall of dust blown by strong winds in deserts called?
questions.fact: Haboob comes from an Arabic word meaning strong wind.

questions.q: What are the warm, dry winds that rush down the eastern side of the Rocky Mountains called?
questions.fact: Chinooks can melt snow so fast that they are nicknamed snow eaters.

questions.q: What is it called when a hurricane pushes ocean water onto land?
questions.fact: Storm surge is often the most dangerous part of a hurricane.

questions.q: Who gives hurricanes their names?
choices: The President of the United States
questions.fact: Names of very deadly hurricanes are retired and never used again.

questions.q: What is the hurricane season in the Atlantic Ocean?
choices: All year with the same chance
questions.fact: Most Atlantic hurricanes happen from August to October.

questions.q: What is the most common type of natural disaster in the world?
questions.fact: Floods affect more people around the world than any other natural disaster.

questions.q: Why is it important to have an emergency kit at home?
choices: To have water, food and supplies if a disaster hits
questions.fact: A kit should have water, food, a flashlight, batteries and first aid supplies.

questions.q: What layer of the atmosphere has the ozone layer in it?
questions.fact: The stratosphere gets warmer as you go higher because ozone soaks up ultraviolet light.

questions.q: What is the outermost layer of Earth's atmosphere, where it fades into space, called?
questions.fact: Some satellites orbit in the exosphere.

questions.q: In which layer of the atmosphere does the International Space Station orbit?
questions.fact: The thermosphere can reach over 1,500 degrees Celsius, but the air is so thin it would not feel hot.

questions.q: What are the two main gases in Earth's air?
questions.fact: Argon is the third most common gas, at about 1 percent.

questions.q: What is the air pressure at sea level like compared to the top of Mount Everest?
questions.fact: Climbers on Everest often carry bottled oxygen because each breath holds about a third as much oxygen.

questions.q: What is the scientific name for the study of Earth's physical features and processes?
questions.fact: Geo comes from the Greek word for Earth.

questions.q: Who is often called the father of modern geology?
questions.fact: In the 1700s, Hutton argued that Earth must be extremely old because rock changes so slowly.

questions.q: What do scientists use to date very old rocks?
choices: Radioactive elements that decay at known rates
questions.fact: This method is called radiometric dating.

questions.q: How long ago did the supercontinent Pangaea begin to break apart?
questions.fact: The breakup of Pangaea created the Atlantic Ocean.

questions.q: Which two continents' coastlines fit together like puzzle pieces?
questions.fact: Matching fossils on both continents also show they were once joined.

questions.q: Which continent has the most people?
questions.fact: As of 2025, more than half of all people on Earth live in Asia.

questions.q: On which continent is the Amazon rainforest?
questions.fact: The Amazon rainforest spreads across nine countries, with the largest part in Brazil.

questions.q: What is light pollution?
choices: Too much artificial light at night that hides the stars
questions.fact: Many people in cities can no longer see the Milky Way because of light pollution.

questions.q: What is the main cause of the seasons being colder at the poles?
choices: They are farther from the Sun
Sunlight hits them at a low angle
questions.fact: Low-angle sunlight spreads its energy over a bigger area, so it heats less.

questions.q: What is the line around the Arctic where the Sun does not set on the summer solstice?
questions.fact: North of the Arctic Circle, there is at least one full day of darkness in winter.

questions.q: What is the name for the green flash that sometimes appears just as the Sun sets over the sea?
questions.fact: It happens because the atmosphere bends green light slightly more than red.

questions.q: What are sundogs?
choices: Bright spots beside the Sun caused by ice crystals
Dogs that sleep in the sun
questions.fact: Sundogs often appear on cold days when thin, icy clouds are in the sky.

questions.q: What is a halo around the Sun or Moon caused by?
questions.fact: A halo often appears when cirrus clouds are in the sky.

questions.q: What does the rhyme red sky at night, sailors' delight usually predict?
questions.fact: A red sunset often means dry air to the west, where weather usually comes from in the middle latitudes.

questions.q: What do we call a region that gets less than about 25 centimeters of rain a year?
questions.fact: Some desert plants can survive for years waiting for the next rain.

questions.q: How do cactus plants survive in the desert?
choices: They store water in their thick stems
questions.fact: Some cactuses have roots that spread out wide just under the surface to catch rain quickly.

questions.q: What is a coral reef's biggest threat as oceans warm?
choices: Too much sunlight on the beach
questions.fact: The Great Barrier Reef has had several mass bleaching events in recent years.

questions.q: What do mangrove forests do for coasts?
choices: Protect them from storms and erosion
questions.fact: Mangrove trees grow in salty water with roots that stick up above the mud.

questions.q: What gas do oceans absorb a lot of, making them more acidic?
questions.fact: Ocean acidification makes it harder for corals and shellfish to build their shells.

questions.q: What fraction of the oxygen we breathe is estimated to come from the ocean?
questions.fact: Tiny ocean plants called phytoplankton make much of this oxygen.

questions.q: What does a national park protect?
questions.fact: Yellowstone, created in 1872, is often called the world's first national park.

questions.q: What is the name of the rock layer under the crust that flows very slowly, like thick putty?
questions.fact: The tectonic plates slide around on top of this soft layer.

questions.q: What kind of seismic waves cannot travel through liquid?
questions.fact: Because S waves do not pass through the outer core, scientists learned it must be liquid.

questions.q: Which earthquake waves arrive first at a seismometer?
questions.fact: P stands for primary because these waves are the fastest.

questions.q: What do we call a crack in Earth's crust where rocks have moved?
questions.fact: Earthquakes happen when rocks along a fault suddenly slip.

questions.q: What is a deep, narrow valley on the ocean floor where one plate sinks under another called?
questions.fact: The sinking of one plate under another is called subduction.

questions.q: What is it called when one tectonic plate slides beneath another?
questions.fact: Subduction zones cause some of the most powerful earthquakes and volcanoes.

questions.q: What is an underwater mountain that does not reach the surface called?
questions.fact: There are thought to be tens of thousands of seamounts in the oceans.

questions.q: What are the wide, flat parts of the deep ocean floor called?
questions.fact: Abyssal plains are among the flattest places on Earth.

questions.q: What is the shallow, gently sloping edge of a continent under the sea called?
questions.fact: Most of the world's fishing happens over continental shelves.

questions.q: How does new ocean floor form?
choices: Magma rises at mid-ocean ridges and cools
questions.fact: This process is called seafloor spreading.

questions.q: What type of volcano is tall and cone-shaped, built from layers of lava and ash?
questions.fact: Mount Fuji and Mount St. Helens are stratovolcanoes.

questions.q: What is the smallest and simplest type of volcano, made of piled-up bits of lava?
questions.fact: Paricutin in Mexico grew from a cornfield in 1943 as a cinder cone.

questions.q: What is a vent in the ground that lets out volcanic gases and steam?
questions.fact: Some fumaroles leave behind yellow crystals of sulfur.

questions.q: What is the hard, ropy kind of lava from Hawaii called?
questions.fact: The rough, jagged kind is called aa, and both names come from the Hawaiian language.

questions.q: Which gas do volcanoes give off the most of?
questions.fact: Volcanoes also give off carbon dioxide and sulfur gases.

questions.q: How can scientists sometimes predict a volcanic eruption?
choices: By watching for small earthquakes and ground swelling
They can always predict the exact day
questions.fact: Volcano monitors also measure gases coming out of the ground.

questions.q: What do we call the remains of a dead plant or animal that has turned to stone?
questions.fact: In petrified wood, minerals slowly replaced the wood, keeping its shape.

questions.q: What is coal made from?
choices: Ancient plants buried and squeezed for millions of years
questions.fact: Much of the world's coal formed from swamp forests about 300 million years ago.

questions.q: How do plant roots help break apart rocks?
choices: They grow into cracks and push them wider
questions.fact: This is a kind of weathering.

questions.q: How does freezing water break rocks?
choices: Water in cracks expands when it freezes
questions.fact: This is called frost wedging, and it also makes potholes in roads.

questions.q: What is the slow downhill creep of soil caused by gravity called?
questions.fact: You can spot soil creep where fences and trees on a hillside lean downhill.

questions.q: Which is heavier, a cubic meter of dry air or a cubic meter of moist air at the same temperature?
questions.fact: Water vapor molecules are lighter than the nitrogen and oxygen molecules they replace.

questions.q: What is the boundary between two air masses called?
questions.fact: Weather often changes quickly when a front passes.

questions.q: What is a warm front?
choices: Warm air sliding up over colder air
questions.fact: Warm fronts often bring long, steady rain.

questions.q: What are the curving lines on a weather map that connect places with equal air pressure called?
questions.fact: When isobars are close together, the wind is strong.

questions.q: What do weather balloons carry into the sky?
choices: Instruments that measure temperature, humidity and wind
questions.fact: Weather balloons are launched around the world twice a day.

questions.q: Which weather satellites stay above one spot on Earth to watch storms?
questions.fact: They orbit about 36,000 kilometers above the equator.

questions.q: What is the cloud type that brings steady rain or snow and is dark and thick?
questions.fact: Nimbus comes from the Latin word for rain cloud.

questions.q: What are the anvil-shaped tops of thunderstorm clouds caused by?
choices: The storm cloud hitting the top of the troposphere and spreading out
Wind blowing them flat from the ground
questions.fact: The rising air cannot easily push into the warmer stratosphere above.

questions.q: What is graupel?
choices: Soft, small pellets of snow and ice
questions.fact: Graupel forms when supercooled water droplets freeze onto snowflakes.

questions.q: What is freezing rain?
choices: Rain that freezes when it hits cold surfaces
questions.fact: Freezing rain can coat roads, trees and power lines in a thick layer of ice.

questions.q: What causes the seasons to be opposite in the Northern and Southern Hemispheres?
choices: The Sun moves north and south
Earth's tilt points one hemisphere toward the Sun while the other points away
questions.fact: In December, the Southern Hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun.

questions.q: What is the main reason it is hotter at the equator than at the poles?
choices: The equator is closer to the Sun's core
Sunlight hits the equator more directly
questions.fact: The same sunlight spread over a larger area at the poles gives less heat.

questions.q: What are thick layers of mud and sand at the bottom of lakes and oceans that build up over time called?
questions.fact: Layers of sediment can hold pollen and tiny shells that reveal past climates.

questions.q: What is the process that turns loose sediment into solid rock?
questions.fact: Minerals in water act like glue to cement the grains together.

questions.q: What metamorphic rock forms when sandstone is heated and squeezed?
questions.fact: Quartzite is very hard and resists weathering.

questions.q: What gives some rocks layers or bands of different colors?
choices: Different materials deposited at different times
questions.fact: Places like the Grand Canyon show millions of years of history in their colored layers.

questions.q: Why do some rocks fizz when a drop of acid touches them?
questions.fact: Geologists use this test to identify limestone and marble.

questions.q: What is the streak test used to identify minerals?
choices: Rubbing a mineral on tile to see the color of its powder
questions.fact: Pyrite looks gold but leaves a greenish black streak.

questions.q: Which element has the chemical symbol O?
questions.fact: Oxygen makes up about 21 percent of the air we breathe.

questions.q: Which element has the chemical symbol Fe?
questions.fact: The symbol Fe comes from ferrum, the Latin word for iron.

questions.q: Which element has the chemical symbol Na?
questions.fact: Na comes from natrium, an old Latin name for sodium.

questions.q: Which element has the chemical symbol Ag?
questions.fact: Ag comes from argentum, the Latin word for silver.

questions.q: Which element has the chemical symbol Pb?
questions.fact: Pb comes from plumbum, the Latin word for lead, which is also where the word plumber comes from.

questions.q: Which element has the chemical symbol K?
questions.fact: Bananas are famous for having a lot of potassium.

questions.q: Which element has the chemical symbol C?
questions.fact: Carbon is in every living thing on Earth.

questions.q: Which element has the chemical symbol Cu?
questions.fact: Cu comes from cuprum, from the Latin name of the island of Cyprus, where copper was mined.

questions.q: Which element has the chemical symbol He?
questions.fact: Helium was found in the Sun's light before it was found on Earth.

questions.q: Which element has the chemical symbol Hg?
questions.fact: Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature.

questions.q: Which element has the chemical symbol Ca?
questions.fact: Calcium helps build strong bones and teeth.

questions.q: Which element has the chemical symbol Cl?
questions.fact: Chlorine is added to swimming pools to kill germs.

questions.q: Which element has the chemical symbol Sn?
questions.fact: Sn comes from stannum, the Latin word for tin.

questions.q: Which element is number 1 on the periodic table?
questions.fact: Hydrogen is the lightest and most common element in the universe.

questions.q: What is the chart that organizes all the chemical elements called?
questions.fact: The periodic table puts elements with similar properties in the same columns.

questions.q: Who created the first widely used periodic table in 1869?
questions.fact: Mendeleev left gaps for elements that had not been discovered yet, and he predicted what they would be like.

questions.q: About how many known elements are there, as of 2025?
questions.fact: As of 2025, 118 elements have been discovered or made in labs.

questions.q: What are the tiny particles with a negative charge that move around an atom's nucleus?
questions.fact: Electrons are about 1,800 times lighter than protons.

questions.q: What are the particles with a positive charge in an atom's nucleus?
questions.fact: The number of protons decides which element an atom is.

questions.q: What particles in an atom's nucleus have no electric charge?
questions.fact: Neutrons were discovered in 1932 by James Chadwick.

questions.q: What is the atomic number of an element?
choices: The number of protons in its atoms
questions.fact: Carbon has atomic number 6, so every carbon atom has 6 protons.

questions.q: What is a molecule?
choices: Two or more atoms joined together
questions.fact: A water molecule is made of two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.

questions.q: What do we call an atom that has gained or lost electrons?
questions.fact: Table salt is made of sodium ions and chloride ions.

questions.q: What is table salt's chemical name?
questions.fact: Sodium alone is a soft metal that reacts wildly with water, and chlorine alone is a poisonous gas.

questions.q: What is the chemical formula for carbon dioxide?
questions.fact: You breathe out carbon dioxide every time you exhale.

questions.q: What is the chemical name for baking soda?
questions.fact: Baking soda releases carbon dioxide bubbles that help cakes rise.

questions.q: What gas is made when you mix baking soda and vinegar?
questions.fact: This reaction is what makes homemade volcanoes fizz.

questions.q: Which gas makes balloons float up in the air?
questions.fact: Helium is lighter than air, so it floats the balloon up.

questions.q: Which noble gas glows red-orange in bright advertising signs?
questions.fact: Other colors in so-called neon signs usually come from different gases or coatings.

questions.q: What is the most common gas in Earth's air after nitrogen?
questions.fact: Nitrogen makes up about 78 percent of the air, and oxygen about 21 percent.

questions.q: Which liquid metal was once used in thermometers?
questions.fact: Mercury is poisonous, so most thermometers now use other liquids or electronics.

questions.q: What is rust?
choices: Iron that has reacted with oxygen and water
questions.fact: The scientific name for rust is iron oxide.

questions.q: Which metal is the best conductor of electricity?
questions.fact: Copper is used in most wires because it is almost as good and much cheaper.

questions.q: Which metal is used most in electrical wires in homes?
questions.fact: Copper bends easily and carries electricity very well.

questions.q: Which metal is light and used to make soda cans?
questions.fact: Aluminum is the most common metal in Earth's crust.

questions.q: Which element is a diamond made of?
questions.fact: Pencil lead, called graphite, is made of carbon too.

questions.q: What is pencil lead actually made of?
questions.fact: Pencils never had real lead in them, the name comes from an old mix-up.

questions.q: Which element is found in computer chips and sand?
questions.fact: Silicon Valley in California got its name from the silicon chips made there.

questions.q: What do we call a substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up?
questions.fact: Enzymes in your body are catalysts that help digest food.

questions.q: What is it called when a solid turns straight into a gas without melting?
questions.fact: Dry ice does this, turning from solid carbon dioxide into a foggy gas.

questions.q: What is dry ice?
choices: Ice that has been dried in the sun
questions.fact: Dry ice is about minus 78 degrees Celsius, so you should never touch it with bare hands.

questions.q: What is it called when a gas turns into a liquid?
questions.fact: Water drops on a cold drink on a hot day come from condensation.

questions.q: What is it called when a liquid turns into a solid?
questions.fact: Water is unusual because it expands when it freezes.

questions.q: At what temperature does water boil at sea level, in Celsius?
questions.fact: High on a mountain, water boils at a lower temperature because the air pressure is lower.

questions.q: At what temperature does water boil at sea level, in Fahrenheit?
questions.fact: Water freezes at 32 degrees Fahrenheit.

questions.q: Why does ice float on water?
choices: Ice is less dense than liquid water
Ice is full of air from bubbles
Water pushes it up with magnets
Ice is lighter because it is cold
questions.fact: This is lucky for fish, because ponds freeze from the top down and the water below stays liquid.

questions.q: What is the coldest possible temperature called?
questions.fact: Absolute zero is about minus 273 degrees Celsius.

questions.q: What is the fourth state of matter, found in lightning and stars?
questions.fact: Plasma is gas that is so hot that electrons get pulled off the atoms.

questions.q: What does a pH below 7 mean?
questions.fact: Lemon juice has a pH of about 2.

questions.q: What does a pH above 7 mean?
questions.fact: Soap and baking soda are bases.

questions.q: Which acid is found in lemons and oranges?
questions.fact: Citric acid gives citrus fruits their sour taste.

questions.q: Which acid is in vinegar?
questions.fact: Vinegar is mostly water with about 5 percent acetic acid.

questions.q: What happens when an acid and a base mix?
questions.fact: Antacid tablets are bases that neutralize extra stomach acid.

questions.q: What does litmus paper do?
choices: Changes color to show if something is an acid or a base
questions.fact: Acids turn blue litmus paper red, and bases turn red litmus paper blue.

questions.q: What is a mixture where one substance dissolves completely into another called?
questions.fact: Salt water is a solution of salt dissolved in water.

questions.q: Which liquid is often called the universal solvent because it dissolves so many things?
questions.fact: Water dissolves more substances than any other common liquid.

questions.q: Why do oil and water not mix?
choices: Water molecules stick to each other but not to oil
questions.fact: Oil floats on top because it is less dense than water.

questions.q: What does density measure?
choices: How much mass is packed into a space
questions.fact: A brick and a sponge can be the same size but have very different densities.

questions.q: What are the units of temperature named after a Swedish scientist?
questions.fact: Anders Celsius created his scale in 1742.

questions.q: Which temperature scale starts at absolute zero?
questions.fact: Scientists use Kelvin because it has no negative numbers.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of force?
questions.fact: One newton is roughly the weight of a small apple.

questions.q: What is the unit used to measure energy?
questions.fact: A joule is named after the English scientist James Prescott Joule.

questions.q: What unit is used to measure electric power?
questions.fact: A typical LED light bulb uses about 10 watts.

questions.q: What unit measures the push of electricity, like on a battery?
questions.fact: A AA battery gives about 1.5 volts.

questions.q: What unit measures how much electric current flows?
questions.fact: The ampere is often shortened to amp.

questions.q: What does hertz measure?
choices: How many times something happens per second
questions.fact: Humans can hear sounds from about 20 to 20,000 hertz.

questions.q: What is the speed of light in empty space, roughly?
questions.fact: Light could circle Earth about seven and a half times in one second.

questions.q: About how fast does sound travel in air?
questions.fact: That is why you see lightning before you hear the thunder.

questions.q: Does sound travel faster in water or in air?
questions.fact: Sound travels about four times faster in water than in air.

questions.q: What do we call an object breaking the sound barrier, which makes a loud boom?
questions.fact: A sonic boom happens when something goes faster than sound.

questions.q: What is an echo?
choices: A sound that gets louder by itself
A sound made by animals only
questions.fact: Bats and dolphins use echoes to find things.

questions.q: What is the loudness of sound measured in?
questions.fact: Sounds above about 85 decibels for a long time can damage your hearing.

questions.q: What do we call sounds too high-pitched for humans to hear?
questions.fact: Doctors use ultrasound to see babies before they are born.

questions.q: What do we call sounds too low-pitched for humans to hear?
questions.fact: Elephants can talk to each other using infrasound over long distances.

questions.q: What happens to light when it passes through a prism?
choices: It splits into a rainbow of colors
questions.fact: Isaac Newton used prisms to show that white light is a mix of colors.

questions.q: What are the colors of the rainbow in order?
choices: Red, yellow, blue, green, orange, purple, pink
Violet, red, green, orange, yellow, blue, indigo
Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, violet
Blue, green, red, yellow, orange, pink, white
questions.fact: Many people remember the order with the name ROY G. BIV.

questions.q: What is the bending of light as it passes from one material into another called?
questions.fact: Refraction is why a straw in a glass of water looks broken.

questions.q: What is light bouncing off a surface called?
questions.fact: A mirror reflects almost all the light that hits it.

questions.q: Why does a red apple look red?
choices: It reflects red light and absorbs other colors
It makes its own red light
Red light is the only light in the room
questions.fact: Without light, nothing would have color at all.

questions.q: Why is the sky blue?
choices: Air scatters blue sunlight more than other colors
questions.fact: This scattering is called Rayleigh scattering.

questions.q: Why are sunsets often red and orange?
choices: The Sun cools down at night
Sunlight passes through more air, which scatters away blue light
questions.fact: At sunset, sunlight travels through much more of the atmosphere to reach your eyes.

questions.q: What type of light can give you a sunburn?
questions.fact: Sunscreen blocks most of the ultraviolet light that burns skin.

questions.q: What type of light can we feel as heat?
questions.fact: Night vision cameras and TV remotes use infrared light.

questions.q: Which type of wave do doctors use to see bones?
questions.fact: X-rays were discovered by Wilhelm Roentgen in 1895.

questions.q: How does a microwave oven heat food?
choices: Its waves make water molecules in the food jiggle
questions.fact: The microwave oven was invented after an engineer noticed a candy bar melted near radar equipment.

questions.q: What is the force that slows down two surfaces rubbing together?
questions.fact: Rubbing your hands together makes them warm because of friction.

questions.q: What is the force that slows things moving through air called?
questions.fact: A parachute works by creating lots of air resistance.

questions.q: What is the upward push that helps things float in water called?
questions.fact: A huge steel ship floats because it pushes aside a lot of water.

questions.q: Which Greek scientist is said to have shouted Eureka in his bath after an idea about floating?
questions.fact: Archimedes realized that the water rising in the tub could measure an object's volume.

questions.q: What does Newton's first law of motion say?
choices: Objects keep doing what they are doing unless a force acts on them
Every object falls at the same speed
questions.fact: This tendency to keep moving or stay still is called inertia.

questions.q: What does Newton's third law of motion say?
choices: Things fall at the same speed
Every action has an equal and opposite reaction
questions.fact: When a rocket pushes gas down, the gas pushes the rocket up.

questions.q: According to a famous story, what fell and helped Isaac Newton think about gravity?
questions.fact: Newton himself told the apple story, but it probably did not hit him on the head.

questions.q: If you drop a bowling ball and a tennis ball at the same time with no air, which lands first?
choices: They land at the same time
questions.fact: Astronaut David Scott showed this on the Moon by dropping a hammer and a feather together.

questions.q: What is the stored energy of an object high up, like a book on a shelf, called?
questions.fact: When the book falls, its potential energy turns into kinetic energy.

questions.q: What is the energy of something that is moving called?
questions.fact: The faster something moves, the more kinetic energy it has.

questions.q: What type of energy is stored in food and batteries?
questions.fact: Your body turns the chemical energy in food into movement and heat.

questions.q: What does the law of conservation of energy say?
choices: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only changed
Energy only comes from the Sun
Energy is the same as mass
questions.fact: When you switch on a lamp, electrical energy changes into light and heat.

questions.q: Which simple machine is a ramp?
questions.fact: Ramps make it easier to lift heavy things by spreading the work over a longer distance.

questions.q: Which simple machine is a seesaw?
questions.fact: A lever turns around a point called a fulcrum.

questions.q: Which simple machine is used to raise a flag up a pole?
questions.fact: A pulley uses a wheel and a rope to change the direction of a pull.

questions.q: Which simple machine is an axe blade?
questions.fact: A wedge turns a downward push into a sideways push that splits things apart.

questions.q: How many classic simple machines are there?
questions.fact: They are the lever, wheel and axle, pulley, inclined plane, wedge and screw.

questions.q: What is the flow of electric charge called?
questions.fact: Electric current in wires is made of moving electrons.

questions.q: What do we call a material that lets electricity flow through it easily?
questions.fact: Most metals are good conductors.

questions.q: What do we call a material that does not let electricity flow easily?
questions.fact: Rubber and plastic are good insulators, which is why wires are covered in them.

questions.q: What is a complete path that electricity flows around called?
questions.fact: If there is a break in the circuit, the electricity stops flowing.

questions.q: What is the kind of electricity that makes your hair stand up when you rub a balloon on it?
questions.fact: Lightning is a giant spark of static electricity.

questions.q: What do opposite magnetic poles do?
questions.fact: Two north poles or two south poles push each other away.

questions.q: What does a compass needle point toward?
questions.fact: A compass works because the needle is a tiny magnet.

questions.q: What do we call a magnet made by running electricity through a coil of wire?
questions.fact: Junkyards use giant electromagnets to lift cars, then switch them off to drop them.

questions.q: Who flew a kite in a storm to show that lightning is electricity, according to a famous story?
questions.fact: Franklin later invented the lightning rod to protect buildings.

questions.q: Which scientist discovered that moving a magnet near a wire makes electricity?
questions.fact: This idea is how power plants and generators make electricity today.

questions.q: What does a light bulb's thin wire, called a filament, do when electricity flows through it?
questions.fact: LED bulbs do not use filaments and waste much less energy as heat.

questions.q: What is Einstein's most famous equation?
questions.fact: It shows that a tiny bit of mass can turn into a huge amount of energy.

questions.q: What is the main kind of energy that nuclear power plants use?
questions.fact: Splitting heavy atoms is called nuclear fission.

questions.q: Which energy source is renewable?
questions.fact: Renewable energy comes from sources that will not run out, like sunlight and wind.

questions.q: Which fossil fuel is a black rock formed from ancient plants?
questions.fact: Coal formed from swamp plants that were buried for millions of years.

questions.q: What do we call energy that comes from the heat inside the Earth?
questions.fact: Iceland gets much of its electricity and heat from geothermal energy.

questions.q: What do we call electricity made from flowing water at dams?
questions.fact: Hydropower has long been one of the world's biggest sources of renewable electricity.

questions.q: What is a scientist who studies living things called?
questions.fact: Biology comes from Greek words meaning the study of life.

questions.q: What is a scientist who studies matter and energy called?
questions.fact: Famous physicists include Isaac Newton and Albert Einstein.

questions.q: What is a scientist who studies plants called?
questions.fact: Botanists have described hundreds of thousands of plant species.

questions.q: What is a scientist who studies animals called?
questions.fact: Zoologists may work in zoos, labs or out in the wild.

questions.q: What is a scientist who studies tiny germs like bacteria called?
questions.fact: Microbiologists help develop medicines and vaccines.

questions.q: What is a scientist who studies dinosaur fossils called?
questions.fact: Archaeologists study things made by people, not dinosaurs.

questions.q: What is the basic unit of all living things?
questions.fact: Some living things, like bacteria, are made of just one cell.

questions.q: Who first named the cell after looking at cork under a microscope in 1665?
questions.fact: Hooke thought the tiny boxes in cork looked like small rooms called cells.

questions.q: Which scientist made very strong early microscopes and first saw bacteria?
questions.fact: Leeuwenhoek called the tiny creatures he saw animalcules.

questions.q: What part of a cell holds its DNA in plants and animals?
questions.fact: The nucleus is often called the cell's control center.

questions.q: Which part of a plant cell captures sunlight to make food?
questions.fact: Chloroplasts are green because they contain chlorophyll.

questions.q: Which part of a cell is often called its powerhouse?
questions.fact: Mitochondria turn food into energy the cell can use.

questions.q: What do plant cells have that animal cells do not?
questions.fact: The stiff cell wall helps plants stand up straight.

questions.q: What does DNA stand for?
questions.fact: DNA carries the instructions for building and running a living thing.

questions.q: What shape is a DNA molecule?
questions.fact: A double helix looks like a twisted ladder.

questions.q: Which scientist's X-ray photo of DNA helped show its double helix shape?
questions.fact: Her famous image is known as Photo 51.

questions.q: Which two scientists described the double helix model of DNA in 1953?
questions.fact: Their model was built using data from Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins.

questions.q: Who is known as the father of genetics for his experiments with pea plants?
questions.fact: Mendel was a monk who grew thousands of pea plants in his garden.

questions.q: What are the sections of DNA that carry instructions for traits like eye color called?
questions.fact: Humans have about 20,000 genes.

questions.q: Who came up with the theory of evolution by natural selection?
questions.fact: Alfred Russel Wallace came up with the same idea around the same time.

questions.q: On which islands did Charles Darwin study finches and giant tortoises?
questions.fact: Darwin visited the Galapagos in 1835 on a ship called HMS Beagle.

questions.q: Which scientist created the system of giving every living thing a two-part Latin name?
questions.fact: Linnaeus published his naming system in the 1700s and named thousands of plants and animals himself.

questions.q: What is the scientific name for humans?
questions.fact: Homo sapiens means wise human in Latin.

questions.q: What are the largest groups that scientists sort living things into, like animals, plants and fungi?
questions.fact: Below kingdom come phylum, class, order, family, genus and species.

questions.q: Which kingdom do mushrooms belong to?
questions.fact: Fungi cannot make their own food from sunlight, so they are not plants.

questions.q: Which tiny living things are made of a single cell with no nucleus?
questions.fact: There are more bacteria in your body than there are people on Earth.

questions.q: Which scientist discovered penicillin, the first antibiotic, in 1928?
questions.fact: Fleming noticed mold had killed bacteria in a dish he forgot to clean.

questions.q: What do antibiotics kill?
questions.fact: Antibiotics do not work on viruses, like the ones that cause colds.

questions.q: Which scientist invented a way to heat milk to kill germs?
questions.fact: The process is called pasteurization after him.

questions.q: Who made the first vaccine, for smallpox, in 1796?
questions.fact: Jenner used material from cowpox, and the word vaccine comes from vacca, Latin for cow.

questions.q: Which disease became the first human disease to be completely wiped out by vaccines?
questions.fact: The World Health Organization declared smallpox eradicated in 1980.

questions.q: Who developed the first successful polio vaccine in the 1950s?
questions.fact: Jonas Salk chose not to patent the vaccine so it could reach more people.

questions.q: What is a virus?
choices: A tiny germ that can only multiply inside living cells
questions.fact: Viruses are much smaller than bacteria and need a microscope called an electron microscope to see.

questions.q: What do plants release into the air during photosynthesis?
questions.fact: Most of the oxygen we breathe came from plants and tiny ocean algae.

questions.q: What green substance in leaves captures sunlight?
questions.fact: In autumn, chlorophyll breaks down and the yellow and orange colors in leaves show through.

questions.q: Which part of a plant takes in water from the soil?
questions.fact: Some tree roots spread much wider than the tree's branches.

questions.q: What are the tiny holes on leaves that let gases in and out called?
questions.fact: A single leaf can have thousands of stomata.

questions.q: What is it called when water evaporates out of a plant's leaves?
questions.fact: A big tree can release hundreds of liters of water into the air on a hot day.

questions.q: What is it called when a seed starts to grow?
questions.fact: Seeds need water, air and the right temperature to germinate.

questions.q: What is it called when pollen moves from one flower to another?
questions.fact: Bees, butterflies, birds, bats and even the wind can pollinate flowers.

questions.q: What part of a flower makes pollen?
questions.fact: The pollen is made in a part at the top of the stamen called the anther.

questions.q: Which tree is the tallest kind in the world?
questions.fact: A coast redwood named Hyperion is over 115 meters tall, as of 2025 the tallest known tree.

questions.q: Which kind of tree is the largest by volume?
questions.fact: A giant sequoia named General Sherman is the largest single-stem tree on Earth by volume.

questions.q: Which plant catches and digests insects with snapping leaves?
